message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and to ensure they receive a safe, habitable living environment. Below is an overview of key tenant rights under Texas law (Texas Property Code, Chapter 24) and related statutes: | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit, two months for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | • Keep records of the unit’s condition at move‑in and move‑out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, and pest control.
• Must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition. | • Report problems promptly; landlords must respond within a reasonable time. | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withholding** | • If landlord fails to repair, tenant may pay the repair cost and deduct it from rent, or withhold rent until repairs are made. | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot disturb the tenant’s peaceful use of the property. | • Unreasonable entry or harassment is prohibited. | | **Entry Notice** | • Landlord must give 24‑hour written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | • Document any unnotified entries. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease must be in writing if the term is longer than one year.
• Landlord cannot impose unreasonable restrictions. | • Review lease carefully; negotiate terms if needed. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • File complaints with the Texas Commission on Human Rights if discrimination occurs. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must provide a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment).
• Eviction requires a court order; landlords cannot forcibly remove tenants. | • Respond to notices promptly; seek legal counsel if threatened with eviction. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control laws. | • Rent increases must comply with lease terms or local ordinances. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential utilities unless otherwise specified. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Tenant Insurance** | • Landlord may require renters’ insurance. | • Obtain coverage to protect personal property. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, move‑in inspection reports, photos, and all communications with the landlord. 2. **Know the Law** – Familiarize yourself with the Texas Property Code, especially Chapters 24 (Residential Landlord‑Tenant Law) and 92 (Discrimination). 3. **Use Written Notices** – When reporting issues, send a written notice (email or certified mail) and keep a copy. 4. **Seek Legal Advice** – If you face eviction or disputes, consult a tenant‑rights attorney or a local legal aid organization. 5. **File Complaints** – For discrimination or habitability violations, file complaints with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the local housing authority. --- #### Quick Reference: What a Landlord Can’t Do - Enter without 24‑hour notice (except emergencies). - Charge more than the statutory security deposit limit. - Force you to pay for normal wear & tear. - Discriminate against you. - Evict you without a court order. If you have a specific situation (e.g., a landlord refusing to make repairs, a dispute over a security deposit, or a threat of eviction), let me know and I can help you draft a formal letter or outline next steps.
